title: The Last Hymn
premise: Beatrix Delacroix, a meticulous property surveyor who survives by staying unremarkable, is sent to appraise the abandoned Halloway house in rural Vermont. The house is alive in ways the paperwork never mentions: mirrors lag a second behind reality, doors refuse to stay counted, and the walls hum with a hymn no one wrote. Beatrix learns that in 1974 the Halloway family's youngest daughter was taken by the house as payment for a bargain her parents made to survive a brutal winter—and the house has been waiting for someone to return what was stolen. To free both the girl and himself, Beatrix must give up his own carefully guarded anonymity and offer the house something it values more than a life: a witness who remembers. In the end, he sings the last hymn with the girl's name restored to it, trading his invisibility for her freedom, and walks out of the house seen—truly seen—for the first time.
about_author: Jonah Ishikawa is a former building inspector from Portland, Oregon, whose decade of crawling through condemned houses left him convinced that old structures hold grudges. He writes horror about places that remember what people would rather forget.

chapters.title: The Appraisal
chapters.summary: Beatrix Delacroix arrives at the Halloway house, a surveyor whose whole life is built on being forgettable. POV: Beatrix. He measures rooms that measure him back, noting doors that won't hold a count. The emotional beat is uneasy professionalism curdling into dread as the house takes an interest in its visitor.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: Beatrix discovers every mirror reflects the room a full second behind reality—and in one reflection, a small figure stands where nothing does. POV: Beatrix. He tries to rationalize it, but the lag grows longer each hour. The beat is denial cracking against evidence, as his invisibility stops protecting him.

chapters.title: The Hymn in the Walls
chapters.summary: At night the house hums a hymn through the plaster, and Beatrix finds sheet music hidden under floorboards, dated 1974, with the final verse torn out. POV: Beatrix. A neighbor, elderly widow Ruth Calloway, warns him off the property. The beat is the pull of curiosity over self-preservation—he stays when he should leave.

chapters.title: What the Calloways Knew
chapters.summary: Ruth confesses: in 1974 the Halloways bargained with the house to survive a killing winter, and it took their daughter, Odile, as payment. POV shifts partly to Ruth's memory. Beatrix realizes the appraisal was never an accident—the house chose him. The beat is guilt and complicity across generations.

chapters.title: Doors That Count Themselves
chapters.summary: Beatrix attempts to leave; the road loops back to the front gate no matter which direction he drives. Inside, the doors now number thirteen where there were twelve. POV: Beatrix. The house is patient, almost gentle, offering warmth and light if he stays. The beat is the seduction of surrender versus the terror of captivity.

chapters.title: Odile
chapters.summary: In the lagging mirror-world, Beatrix meets Odile—a child frozen at nine years old, fifty years hungry, who mistakes him for her brother. POV alternates between Beatrix and Odile's mirror-perspective. She shows him the torn hymn verse hidden inside herself. The beat is tenderness blooming in a haunted place: found family forming between captor's hostage and intruder.

chapters.title: The Price of Survival
chapters.summary: Beatrix researches the Halloway bargain and finds the house doesn't want a replacement—it wants completion of the original debt, plus interest accrued over fifty years. POV: Beatrix. The house begins taking pieces of him: memories, then his reflection entirely. The beat is desperation sharpening into resolve as time visibly runs out.

chapters.title: Thirteen Doors
chapters.summary: Beatrix opens the thirteenth door, which appears only at 3:14 a.m., and finds the room where the bargain was signed—his own name already inked into a ledger beneath the Halloways'. POV: Beatrix. The house offers him Odile's freedom if he takes her place permanently. The beat is the cruelest choice: love against duty, survival against sacrifice.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: Refusing both bargains, Beatrix instead reconstructs the torn verse from Odile's memory and Ruth's recollection, and at dawn sings the completed hymn aloud in the parlor—naming Odile, witnessing her, refusing to let the house keep what was never given freely. POV: Beatrix, with the house itself answering. The climax: the mirrors snap into real-time, and the house convulses around them.

chapters.title: Seen
chapters.summary: The house releases Odile, aging her gently into the woman she should have become, and lets Beatrix go—but keeps his reflection as a permanent resident, a fair trade he accepts willingly. POV: Beatrix, closing the appraisal file marked 'inhabited.' The resolution: walking out truly visible, changed, with a new family waiting in the daylight and a hymn finally finished.
